name: Navy Rum
description: The Royal Navy's daily rum ration, blended dark and bottled at 54.5% — the strength at which spilled spirit still lets gunpowder ignite. The tot was abolished on 31 July 1970, remembered as Black Tot Day.
funFact: Proof was originally tested by soaking gunpowder in the rum and lighting it — if it burned, the spirit was above proof and the purser had not watered it.

serve.how: Neat or over a single cube. It is the correct rum for a Grog — rum, water, lime and sugar — which the Navy introduced in 1740 specifically to stop sailors hoarding their ration and drinking it all at once.

composition.summary: A blend of heavy pot-still rums from across the Caribbean, bottled at overproof strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses rums from Guyana, Trinidad, Barbados and Jamaica

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, blended for consistency rather than age

composition.process: The blend was specified by the Admiralty, which is why it is a style rather than a place.

name: Solera Rum
description: Aged by the fractional system borrowed from sherry, where casks are partly emptied and topped from younger ones so no vintage stands alone. Rich and sweet, and a source of endless argument about age statements.
funFact: A solera number usually refers to the oldest drop in the system, not the youngest, which is why a 23 on the label means something quite different from a Scotch age statement.

serve.glass: Snifter or rocks glass with one cube
serve.how: Neat or over one large cube. These are sweet, often with added sugar, so treat them as dessert spirits rather than mixing rums. An orange twist lifts the butterscotch.

composition.summary: Molasses rum matured through a fractional blending system.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera criaderas, casks partially emptied and refilled

composition.process: Because casks are never fully emptied, the system contains a trace of every year it has run.

name: Rhum Vieux Agricole
description: Cane-juice rum aged at least three years in small oak, the top tier of the Martinique AOC. Keeps the grassy vegetal signature of agricole underneath genuine cask depth — a combination nothing else offers.
funFact: The Martinique AOC regulates cane variety, harvest timing, fermentation length and still design, making it easily the strictest rum appellation in the world.

serve.how: Neat, in a tulip, no ice — this is the rum that most rewards being treated like a cognac. The grassiness that survives ageing is the point, and dilution buries it.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice distilled in a creole column and aged three years or more.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in oak under 650 litres

composition.process: Small casks and tropical heat mean a three-year vieux carries more wood than a decade-old continental spirit.

name: Rhum Blanc Agricole
description: Unaged cane-juice rum, rested a few months in steel and bottled at 50% or more. Intensely grassy, olive-brined and vegetal — the purest expression of what fresh cane actually tastes like.
funFact: AOC rules require it to rest at least three months before bottling, purely to let the harshest volatiles blow off.

serve.how: In a Ti' Punch: a spoon of cane syrup, a disc of lime peel squeezed and dropped in, then the rhum, no ice. That is the drink the category exists for, and locals mix it themselves at the table.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented briefly and column-distilled, unaged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cane juice from AOC-designated varieties

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three months in inert vessels

composition.process: Short fermentation, often under 48 hours, is what preserves the grassy character.

name: Rhum Élevé Sous Bois
description: The middle grade of agricole: at least a year in wood but not the three required for vieux. Straw-gold, lightly oaked, and the everyday sipping rhum of the French islands.
funFact: Also sold as rhum paille — straw rum — for its colour, which sits between the white and the vieux in every sense.

serve.how: Neat or over ice. It makes a rounder Ti' Punch than the white, and it is the grade islanders reach for when the white is too fierce and the vieux too precious.

composition.summary: Cane-juice rum aged between one and three years in oak.
composition.process: The category exists because three years of tropical ageing loses a great deal to evaporation.

name: Cachaça de Alambique
description: Pot-distilled artisanal cachaça, as opposed to the industrial column-distilled kind that fills most caipirinhas. Made in small batches on farms, and a completely different drink from the mass-market version.
funFact: Minas Gerais alone has thousands of registered alambique producers, most of them family operations distilling from their own cane.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, which is how it is drunk in Minas. Using a good alambique cachaça in a caipirinha is not wrong, but the lime will flatten nuances you have paid for.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented with wild yeast and pot-distilled in small batches.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, heads and tails discarded by hand

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often rested in native Brazilian woods

composition.process: The cut is made by the distiller's judgement rather than automatically, which is the whole difference in quality.

name: Ron Añejo
description: The Spanish-Caribbean aged style: column-distilled, oak-matured for several years, and finished light and smooth rather than heavy. The house style across Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela.
funFact: Tropical ageing loses up to eight per cent a year to evaporation, against around two per cent in Scotland — which is why old Caribbean rum is scarce.

serve.how: Neat or over one large cube. The Spanish style is built for easy drinking rather than for standing up to mixers, so a Cuba Libre made with it tastes noticeably better than one made with a heavier rum.

composition.summary: Molasses rum column-distilled to a light spirit and oak-aged.
composition.process: Light distillation plus charcoal filtration is the Cuban template that the whole Spanish style follows.

name: Wedderburn Rum
description: The heaviest classical Jamaican mark, made with long fermentation and dunder to build enormous ester levels. Overwhelmingly fruity and funky, and used in tiny proportions to flavour blends.
funFact: Jamaican rum is classified by ester count in grams per hectolitre of pure alcohol; Wedderburn sits high, and Continental Flavoured higher still, up to a legal ceiling of 1,600.

serve.how: A very small pour neat if you want to understand it, but its real job is blending — a teaspoon transforms a whole tiki drink. Treat it as a flavouring agent with alcohol attached.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented long with dunder and muck, then pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Molasses, dunder pit acids, cane vinegar

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often unaged for blending; aged versions exist

composition.process: Dunder — the acidic residue from the previous distillation — is recycled to drive ester formation.

name: Plummer Rum
description: The medium-ester Jamaican mark, sitting between light Common Clean and heavy Wedderburn. Fruity and characterful without being overwhelming, and the backbone of many classic Jamaican blends.
funFact: The mark names — Plummer, Wedderburn, Common Clean — come from nineteenth-century estates and have outlived most of the plantations themselves.

serve.how: Neat or over ice; it is drinkable in a way the high-ester marks are not. In a Mai Tai or a Planter's Punch it gives Jamaican character without dominating the glass.

composition.summary: Molasses fermented at medium length and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Ester level is controlled by fermentation length and the amount of dunder returned to the wash.

name: Blackstrap Rum
description: Made from the final, most exhausted grade of molasses — nearly black, bitter and mineral. Heavier and less sweet than dark rum, and the defining ingredient in a Corn 'n' Oil.
funFact: Blackstrap is the third boiling of sugarcane syrup, so depleted of sugar that it is more often sold as animal feed than as food.

serve.how: In a Corn 'n' Oil with falernum and lime, which is Barbados' own drink and the best use of it. A float on a tiki build adds depth and colour. Neat it is challenging and genuinely bitter.

composition.summary: Final-grade blackstrap molasses fermented and distilled.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some oak; colour is mostly from the base

composition.process: Very little residual sugar means the flavour is mineral and bitter rather than sweet.

name: Panamanian Rum
description: Light column-still rum aged in the tropics, shaped heavily by Cuban master distillers who settled in Panama. Smooth, vanilla-forward and often finished in wine or sherry casks.
funFact: Don Pancho Fernández, who shaped much of Panama's modern rum, trained in Cuba and ran the state rum industry there before emigrating.

serve.how: Neat or over one cube. Panamanian rum is soft enough to sip young, and the sherry- and port-finished expressions are worth seeking out for anyone who finds Spanish-style rum too plain.

composition.summary: Molasses column-distilled and tropically aged in Panama.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon, with sherry and wine finishes common

composition.process: Cuban technical lineage is why it tastes closer to Havana than to its Central American neighbours.

name: Venezuelan Rum
description: Protected by a national denomination of origin requiring at least two years in oak, which is stricter than most rum-producing countries manage. Rich, round and often criticised for added sugar.
funFact: The Ron de Venezuela DO sets a two-year minimum for everything, including the white rums, which most producing nations do not require at all.

serve.how: Neat or over a large cube. Many bottlings carry significant added sugar, which makes them dessert spirits — worth knowing before judging one against a dry agricole.

composition.summary: Molasses rum distilled and aged at least two years under national DO rules.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum two years, ex-bourbon and ex-whisky oak

composition.process: Blending pot and column is common here, which gives more body than the pure Spanish style.

name: Nicaraguan Rum
description: Aged in the shadow of the San Cristóbal volcano, using water filtered through volcanic rock. Light and clean in the Spanish style, with slow-fermented molasses giving more fruit than most.
funFact: Flor de Caña's distillery sits at the foot of an active volcano and the company plants a tree for every barrel it fills.

serve.how: Neat or over ice. The older expressions carry no added sugar, which makes them drier than their Venezuelan and Guatemalan neighbours and better suited to sipping.

composition.summary: Slow-fermented molasses column-distilled and tropically aged.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak; no sugar added to the aged range

composition.process: Fermentation runs longer than the regional norm, which builds fruit esters before distillation.

name: Dominican Rum
description: One of the three Caribbean rum traditions with protected status, alongside Cuba and Jamaica. Dry and light in the Spanish manner, with a national DO covering everything made on the island.
funFact: The DO requires a minimum of one year in oak for anything called Dominican rum, white expressions included.

serve.how: Neat, over ice, or in a Santo Libre with lime and lemon-lime soda, which is what Dominicans actually drink. The aged expressions sip well without being sweetened into submission.

composition.summary: Molasses rum column-distilled and aged under the national DO.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum one year; premium expressions far longer

composition.process: The island's rum tradition dates to the earliest sugar plantations in the Americas.

name: Cañazo
description: Peru's artisanal cane spirit, distilled in the Andean valleys and the highland cousin of coastal pisco. Long dismissed as a peasant drink and now being bottled seriously for the first time.
funFact: Cane grows in the warm Andean valleys at altitudes where grapes will not, which is why Peru has two entirely separate distilling traditions.

serve.how: Neat, or with lime and sugar in the highland manner. It has the grassy character of an agricole rum with a mineral edge from altitude, and works well anywhere you would use white rum.

composition.summary: Andean cane juice fermented and pot-distilled at altitude.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cane juice from Andean valleys

composition.process: Distilling at altitude lowers the boiling point, which producers say gives a lighter spirit.

name: Rhum de Marie-Galante
description: From a small round island off Guadeloupe with three working distilleries and a tradition of bottling at 59%. Fiercely aromatic cane-juice rum, and the strongest agricole regularly made.
funFact: The island's habit of bottling at 59% rather than the usual 50% is purely local custom, and islanders consider anything weaker to be watered.

serve.how: In a Ti' Punch, made with a light hand — at 59% the usual measure is too much. Locals drink it that way and adjust the cane syrup upward rather than the rum down.

composition.summary: Fresh cane juice fermented and column-distilled, bottled overproof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh cane juice grown on the island

components.label: Aging
components.detail: White, élevé sous bois and vieux all produced

composition.process: Three distilleries on one small island, each with a distinctly different house style.

name: Mezcal Espadín
description: Made from Agave angustifolia, the cultivated workhorse behind around ninety per cent of all mezcal. Matures in six to eight years, which is fast for agave, and is the baseline against which every wild varietal is judged.
funFact: Espadín is the same species as the blue Weber used for tequila is closely related to, and it is the only agave farmed at real scale for mezcal.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, in a wide shallow glass, sipped rather than shot. Orange slices with sal de gusano are the traditional accompaniment in Oaxaca. Never chill it.

composition.summary: Cultivated Espadín agave pit-roasted, crushed and twice pot-distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pit-roasted, tahona-crushed, copper or clay pot stills

composition.process: Earth-pit roasting over hot stones is where all the smoke comes from — nothing is added.

name: Mezcal Tepeztate
description: From a wild agave that grows sideways out of cliff faces and takes up to twenty-five years to mature. Herbaceous, vegetal and unlike anything else — one of the most distinctive spirits made anywhere.
funFact: Tepeztate can take a quarter of a century to flower, which means a bottle drunk today comes from a plant that started growing before the mezcal boom existed.

serve.how: Neat and unhurried, in small sips. The vegetal, almost savoury profile confounds people expecting smoke and sweetness. It is a spirit to sit with rather than to introduce anyone to the category with.

composition.summary: Wild Tepeztate agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Maturation times this long make sustainable harvesting a genuine and unresolved problem.

name: Mezcal Madrecuixe
description: A wild agave with a long narrow trunk rather than a round heart, giving a mineral, almost saline mezcal. Twelve to fifteen years to maturity and harvested from the hillsides rather than farmed.
funFact: Madrecuixe is one of several karwinskii agaves whose long trunks look more like small trees than the rosette shape most people picture.

serve.how: Neat, small sips, at room temperature. The mineral quality is the signature and comes through most clearly on an empty palate — taste it before richer mezcals, not after.

composition.summary: Wild Madrecuixe agave roasted and pot-distilled.
composition.process: The trunk holds less sugar than a round piña, so yields are low and prices high.

name: Mezcal Arroqueño
description: A huge wild agave, sometimes over two metres across, taking fifteen to twenty-five years to mature. Sweet, earthy and full-bodied, with a richness the smaller agaves cannot reach.
funFact: Arroqueño is an ancestor of Espadín and one of the largest agaves used for mezcal, with single plants weighing hundreds of kilos.

serve.how: Neat and slowly. Its size means one plant yields a lot of spirit, but the decades to maturity keep it rare. Richer and sweeter than the karwinskii agaves, so serve it later in a tasting.

composition.summary: Wild Arroqueño agave roasted, crushed and pot-distilled.
composition.process: As a genetic parent of Espadín it shows the sweetness that cultivation selected for.

name: Mezcal Cuishe
description: Another long-trunked karwinskii agave, giving a mezcal that is dry, herbal and faintly medicinal. Around twelve years to maturity and almost entirely wild-harvested.
funFact: The karwinskii family — cuishe, madrecuixe, barril, tobasiche — are all closely related and locals distinguish them by trunk length and where on the hillside they grow.

serve.how: Neat, small pours. Drier and more austere than Espadín, and it makes an excellent bridge between the cultivated and wild styles for someone working through a flight.

composition.summary: Wild Cuishe agave pit-roasted and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Producers often distil the different karwinskii varieties separately purely to show the differences.

name: Mezcal Ensamble
description: Made by roasting and fermenting several agave varieties together, rather than blending finished spirits. A deliberate composition, and often how a producer uses a small wild harvest that could not fill a batch alone.
funFact: An ensamble differs from a blend: the agaves are combined before roasting, so they ferment and distil as one rather than being married afterwards.

serve.how: Neat, at room temperature. Ensambles are often more complex than any single varietal in them, and they are usually the best value in a producer's range because wild agave goes further.

composition.summary: Several agave species roasted, fermented and distilled together.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Two or more agave species, typically Espadín plus wild varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Combined before roasting, then distilled as one batch

composition.process: Combining before roasting rather than after distilling is what makes it an ensamble and not a blend.

name: Destilado de Agave
description: Agave spirit made outside the mezcal denomination — from the wrong state, the wrong paperwork or an unapproved method. Often identical in quality and sometimes better, but legally forbidden the name.
funFact: Several Mexican states with centuries of agave distilling — including Jalisco outside the tequila zone — fall outside the mezcal DO entirely, so their spirits cannot be called mezcal.

serve.how: Neat, as you would any mezcal. The label tells you about regulation rather than quality, and some of the most interesting agave spirits in Mexico sit in this category by geography alone.

composition.summary: Agave roasted, fermented and distilled outside the DO's boundaries.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Any agave species, cultivated or wild

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Traditional pit-roast and pot still, usually

composition.process: The category exists because denominations of origin draw lines on maps, not around traditions.
